name: Secular state
scope: The secular state as a form of state in its relation to religion: a state that is officially neutral on religion, establishes neither a religion nor atheism, keeps its legal and judicial processes out of the control of religious institutions, and deals with every citizen as a citizen irrespective of religion (Kuru's two criteria; Donald Smith's working definition, which adds guaranteed freedom of religion for individuals and groups; Bhargava's account of a state whose ends, institutions, and law and policy are disconnected from religion; An-Na'im's 'neutral regarding religious doctrine'; Guzek's reading of it as a proposal for ordering relations among citizens of different religions). The defining sources name several strands of it and treat them as varieties of one thing: the passive, separationist model (the United States), the assertive laicist model that confines religion to the private sphere (France, Turkey), mutual-exclusion 'wall of separation' secularism versus the Indian 'neutrality toward religion' model that protects all religions and favours none (Nehru's dharma nirapeksha), and the secular state argued for in Muslim-majority societies (An-Na'im). The sources set it apart from theocracy, from states with an established religion or church, and from antireligious (state-atheist) states. The thinkers they tie to it are those who argued for or defined it, above all Nehru for India; the texts are Donald Smith's India as a Secular State, Lanka Sundaram's A Secular State for India (1944) and An-Na'im's Islam and the Secular State. Lists of which countries are secular states, adherents' party platforms, and other writings by these authors answer nothing here.

sources.title: Passive and Assertive Secularism: Historical Conditions, Ideological Struggles, and State Policies toward Religion (Ahmet T. Kuru, World Politics 59, July 2007; copy hosted at San Diego State University)
sources.author: Ahmet T. Kuru
sources.usedFor: Criteria for a secular state and its difference from religious, established-church and antireligious states; passive versus assertive secular states.

sources.title: Political Secularism: Why It Is Needed and Why We Need to Learn from Its Distinctive Indian Version (Rajeev Bhargava, 2006; SSOAR copy)
sources.author: Rajeev Bhargava
sources.usedFor: What distinguishes a secular state from a theocracy and from states with established religions; varieties of secular state; the Indian model.

sources.title: India as a Secular State (Donald Eugene Smith, Princeton University Press, 1963; Digital Library of India scan on archive.org)
sources.author: Donald Eugene Smith
sources.usedFor: Working definition of the secular state and its three sets of relations (religion and the individual, the state and the individual, the state and religion); Nehru's and Gandhi's conceptions; Sundaram's 1944 book.

sources.title: Secularism | Definition, Separation of Church and State, History, Varieties, & Facts (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.usedFor: Nehru's ideal of a secular state as neutrality toward religion; Turkey as an explicitly secular republic.

sources.title: Mediatizing Secular State: Media, Religion and Politics in Contemporary Poland (Damian Guzek, Peter Lang, 2019; open access, archive.org copy of the OAPEN edition), ch. 1.2 'Understanding the secular state'
sources.author: Damian Guzek
sources.usedFor: Scholarly discussion of what the notion of a secular state covers (laïcité, worldview neutrality, church-state models).

sources.title: Nehru and the Secular State of India (Victor Z. Narivelil, MA thesis, Loyola University; archive.org copy), ch. II 'Nehru's ideal of the secular state'
sources.author: Victor Z. Narivelil
sources.usedFor: Nehru's conception of the secular state: protects all religions, favours none, equal rights irrespective of religion.

sources.title: Islam and the Secular State: Negotiating the Future of Shari'a (Abdullahi Ahmed An-Na'im, Harvard University Press, 2008; archive.org copy), ch. 1 'Why Muslims Need a Secular State'
sources.author: Abdullahi Ahmed An-Na'im
sources.usedFor: A thinker's own account of the secular state: neutral regarding religious doctrine, enforcing no religious law, open to religion in politics.

sources.title: A Secular State for India: Thoughts on India's Political Future (Lanka Sundaram, Rajkamal Publications, 1944; archive.org copy)
sources.author: Lanka Sundaram
sources.usedFor: The 1944 argument for a secular state and constitution for India, against religion as the foundation of the state.

name: Laicist state
aliases.quote: In addition, the laicist state does not give privileges to any one religion or concept of a good life but grants everyone freedom within set limits.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) argues there should be no penal or other legal consequences for apostasy, because belief presupposes free choice, and urges abolishing the notion.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) calls for Muslims to reinterpret historical Shari'a principles such as qawama, dhimma and violently aggressive jihad, because they reflect the social and economic realities of their time.

civil-marriage.rationale: Smith (ch. 'Religion, Law, and Secularism') describes the Special Marriage Act as a civil code in embryo that lets Indians marry civilly without giving up their religion.

clerical-rule.rationale: Bhargava sets the secular state apart from a theocracy run by a priestly order claiming a divine commission, and An-Na'im (ch. 1) rejects an Islamic state that enforces Shari'a.

communal-electorates.rationale: Sundaram (Book II, 'The Citadel of Citizenship') demands the destruction of separate electorates as a poison, Narivelil (ch. II) shows Nehru calling them harmful, and Smith (ch. on Constitutional Reforms) says separate representation encouraged communalism.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says the democratic state derives its authority from the consent of the governed, a secular source.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) says human rights and fundamental constitutional rights should not normally be subject to the will of the majority, at least not by a simple majority vote.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 6) says democracy is rule by the majority only provided that the rights of the minority, even of one person, are respected, so elections alone do not suffice.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says the state's authority comes from a secular source and is not subordinate to ecclesiastical power, and An-Na'im (ch. 1) says what a state enforces in the name of Shari'a is political will, not divine authority.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) says human rights are protected through a constitutional bill of rights or constitutional organization of the state, so as to entrench them against the contingencies of politics and the will of a simple majority.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says any state discrimination on the basis of religion runs counter to the secular state, and An-Na'im (ch. 1) says no state may violate constitutionalism, human rights and citizenship.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) defines the secular state as one that guarantees both individual and corporate freedom of religion, so religious groups hold rights as well as individuals.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Smith (ch. 'Religion, Law, and Secularism') presents the personal-law bars on marriage across religious lines as restrictive provisions that the Special Marriage Act was passed to get around.

islam-incompatible.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) says he is not suggesting that any conception of Shari'a is inherently incompatible with constitutionalism, human rights and citizenship, only certain traditional interpretations, and he calls these norms neither alien nor irrelevant to Asian and African societies.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) holds that no specific religious doctrine may be enforced as state policy or law just because believers hold it, and Bhargava separates the secular state from the theocracy governed by divine laws.

morality-needs-religion.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) says secularism needs religion as a widely accepted source of moral guidance for the political community.

more-religion-public.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) gives religion a public role in shaping policy through civic reason and Bhargava's Indian model is not hostile to its public presence, whereas Sundaram (Book I) keeps religion a private matter between a person and God, apart from politics.

national-church-status.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says a state church runs against the secular state, Kuru's criteria require no established religion, and Bhargava says secular states refuse to establish or disestablish religions.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Sundaram (Book II, 'The Citadel of Citizenship') wants differentiation between people by religion removed from politics, and Smith (ch. on separate electorates) says separate representation stimulated communalism.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Bhargava lists no compulsion to receive religious instruction among the marks of a secular state, and Narivelil (ch. IV) cites Art. 28 barring religious instruction in wholly state-funded schools.

one-party-rule.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) says majority rule cannot mean that a political majority takes over the institutions of the state to the exclusion of other political forces.

population-transfer.rationale: Narivelil (ch. II) reports Nehru refusing Hindu communal demands for an exchange of population on a religious basis as fantastic and opposed to all the ideals free India is committed to, and Smith (ch. 1) makes citizenship irrespective of religion part of the secular state.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) finds no Qur'anic offense or penalty of blasphemy and says there should be no penal consequences for apostasy and its related concepts.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) calls for reinterpreting Shari'a on male guardianship, the sovereignty of Muslims over non-Muslims and aggressive jihad, arguing they reflect the conditions of their time.

religion-illusion.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) defines the secular state as one 'neutral regarding religious doctrine', and Kuru separates it from antireligious states, so it takes no side on whether religion is an illusion.

religions-one-truth.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) defines the secular state as one 'neutral regarding religious doctrine', and Kuru describes passive secularism as state neutrality toward religions, so the state takes no side on whether religions share one truth.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Kuru's passive secular states (the United States) allow religious dress while assertive ones (France, Turkey) ban it, Guzek (ch. 1.2) contrasts open separation with hostile laicite, and An-Na'im (ch. 1) criticises the French headscarf ban as a breach of civic reason.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) says secularism precludes any specific understanding of religious doctrine from being directly enforced as state policy.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Smith (ch. 'Constitutional Framework') holds that freedom of religion gives way to public order and general law, and that optional practices need no protection, while Guzek (ch. 1.4) shows secular states accommodating religion through conscientious exemptions in several competing ways.

religious-nation.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) makes citizenship irrespective of religion a component of the secular state, Bhargava says no religious community can claim the state as its own, and Narivelil (ch. II) gives Nehru's equal rights irrespective of religion.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) says violently aggressive jihad must be reformed, and Sundaram (Book I) lists the Muslim jihad among the political failures of religion in politics.

reserved-seats-excluded-groups.rationale: Smith (ch. on caste) says reserved legislative seats for Scheduled Castes are in logical contradiction with the secular principle that the state deals with the individual only as a citizen, and grants them only as a temporary measure with some merit.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Narivelil (ch. III) calls freedom of religion an absolute requirement of the secular state and shows Nehru fighting the Indian Converts bill and every attempt to restrict propagation, and Smith (ch. 'Propagation of Religion') records the same bill's defeat as unconstitutional.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says the state's authority comes from a secular source and is not subordinate to ecclesiastical power, and An-Na'im (ch. 2) treats the Fatimid claim of a 'divine right to rule' as invalid and unrealistic.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) defines the secular state as one 'neutral regarding religious doctrine', and Kuru describes passive secularism as state neutrality toward religions, so the state takes no side on whether scripture is error-free.

separate-church-state.rationale: The sources split on 'strictly': Sundaram (Book I) wants religion divorced from politics and citizenship, while Bhargava, An-Na'im (ch. 1) and Kuru (note 2) reject strict or mutual-exclusion separation for principled distance or minimal neutrality.

separated-powers.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) names the separation of powers and the independence of the judiciary as constitutional principles to be upheld, saying some arrangements are too inadequate to uphold them.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) names male guardianship of women (qawama) as a traditional principle that needs significant reform, because it reflects the conditions of its time and not the message of Islam.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Kuru defines the secular state as one that establishes neither an official religion nor atheism and separates it from antireligious states, and Bhargava rejects hostility to religion.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Guzek (ch. 1.3) says the laicist state does not give privileges to any one religion or concept of a good life but grants everyone freedom within set limits.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Smith (ch. 1) says it is not the state's function to regulate or direct religion and that religious groups run themselves, subject only to general laws, and Guzek (ch. 1.2) describes the secular state as abstaining from interfering in the internal affairs of religious associations.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Smith (ch. 'Religion, Law, and Secularism') treats religion-based personal laws as contrary to the secular state and a uniform code as the aim to be reached by stages, Sundaram (Book II, 'The Citadel of Citizenship') wants a generic law for every man, woman and child, and Narivelil (ch. II) calls religious personal law an obstacle to secular democracy.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Guzek (ch. 1.2) describes the secular state as abstaining from interfering in the internal affairs of religious associations, and Smith (ch. 1) says religious groups run themselves subject only to general law, so it takes no side on who may hold religious office.

women-must-cover.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 1) says dress style normally stays a matter of free choice, so women can neither be forced to wear the veil nor prevented from wearing it.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3 and ch. 4) lists inheritance among the matters where traditional Shari'a gives women unequal rights, and he faults Indian state secularism for giving Hindu women an inheritance share but not Muslim women.

women-suffrage.rationale: An-Na'im (ch. 3) objects that traditional readings of Shari'a deny women public office over men and restrict their constitutional rights, and holds that citizens' constitutional and human rights apply to men and women equally and without discrimination.

summary: A secular state is one that is officially neutral on religion: it establishes neither a religion nor atheism, keeps its courts and laws out of religious institutions' hands, guarantees freedom of religion, and treats every citizen as a citizen whatever their faith. The sources differ over how far apart the two should sit, from Sundaram's divorce of religion from politics and the American wall, through Nehru's neutrality and Bhargava's principled distance, to An-Na'im's secular state that leaves religion a voice in public debate.

furtherReading.title: Secularism (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
furtherReading.note: A short overview of secularism and the separation of religion and state, with the Indian debates.

furtherReading.title: Passive and Assertive Secularism (Ahmet Kuru)
furtherReading.note: Defines the secular state and sets the American, French and Turkish models side by side.

furtherReading.title: Political Secularism (Rajeev Bhargava)
furtherReading.note: Separates the secular state from theocracy and established religion and sets out principled distance.

furtherReading.title: India as a Secular State (Donald Eugene Smith)
furtherReading.note: The classic book-length account, opening with a working definition of the secular state.

notes: Only religion-and-state statements are answered; economic, ecological and other statements are null because the sources do not take positions on them. Women's rights, family-law and other social-reform statements are left null: Smith (ch. 'Religion, Law, and Secularism') says the Hindu Code debate was not about the secular state, and An-Na'im says secularism alone does not settle them. Items in Congress's 1931 Karachi resolution are treated as that party's programme, not as tenets of the secular state. 'Strictly separate' is scored 0 because the sources split between strict separation (Sundaram, the American wall) and principled distance or neutrality (Bhargava, An-Na'im, Nehru). Catholic-Orthodox and other books found by title (Runciman, Strachan, Divine Rulers in a Secular State) are church history or anthropology and were not used.
